entries.name: The three-step pattern a session runs in

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Rhythm of Play / p. 5

entries.evidence: The three main pillars of D&D play are social interaction, exploration, and combat. Whichever one you’re experiencing, the game unfolds according to this basic pattern:
entries.note: Declined, not missed. The pattern is what the people at the table do -- the GM describes, the players say what their characters do, the GM narrates -- and each step is an act of description or judgement, not a computation over a state an engine holds. An engine answers questions inside step 3, and the loop around it is the table's. OutsideCurrentScope.

entries.name: An exception beats the general rule it contradicts

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Exceptions Supersede General Rules / p. 5

entries.evidence: General rules govern each part of the game. For example, the combat rules tell you that melee attacks use Strength and ranged attacks use Dexterity. That’s a general rule, and a general rule is in effect as long as something in the game doesn’t explicitly say otherwise. The game also includes elements—class features, feats, weapon properties, spells, magic items, monster abilities, and the like—that sometimes contradict a general rule. When an exception and a general rule disagree, the exception wins.
entries.note: The precedence rule of the whole corpus, and the reason no mapped rule here can be read alone: every general rule in this map is defeasible by an element outside it. A test must show that where two rules the engine holds disagree and one is an exception, the exception's answer is returned, and that the engine can say which rule it applied. The corpus names the classes of element that carry exceptions -- class features, feats, weapon properties, spells, magic items, monster abilities -- and every one is outside this slice, so what the engine can hold today is the rule, not its instances.

entries.name: A fraction rounds down unless a rule says to round up

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Round Down / p. 5

entries.evidence: Whenever you divide or multiply a number in the game, round down if you end up with a fraction, even if the fraction is one-half or greater. Some rules make an exception and tell you to round up.
entries.note: The corpus prints this rule twice, identically: here as a sidebar on p. 5, and again in the Rules Glossary on p. 187 where trial 8 cites it. 0030 settles a repeated passage by the container its citation names, and the container this grammar has is the heading path -- which cannot separate these two, because `Playing the Game` precedes both printings. The citation is written as this slice's own printing requires; #433's second hypothesis is what it is for.

locator.citation: Playing the Game / D20 Tests / p. 6

entries.evidence: When the outcome of an action is uncertain, the game uses a d20 roll to determine success or failure. These rolls are called D20 Tests, and they come in three kinds: ability checks, saving throws, and attack rolls. They follow these steps:
entries.note: The corpus's own three-way classification, and a closed one: a test must assert exactly three kinds. Everything downstream in this slice that rolls a d20 is one of them, which is why this entry is the root of the D20 Test subtree rather than the steps that follow it.

entries.name: Roll, add modifiers, compare to a target number

locator.citation: Playing the Game / D20 Tests / p. 6

crossReferences.cites: described later in “Playing the Game”
crossReferences.unmapped: Advantage and Disadvantage are defined on p. 7, inside this slice, and are `advantage-disadvantage`; the phrase is the corpus pointing forward, and the pointer is answered there.

entries.evidence: 4: Roll 1d20. You always want to roll high. If the roll has Advantage or Disadvantage (described later in “Playing the Game”), you roll two d20s, but you use the number from only one of them— the higher one if you have Advantage or the lower one if you have Disadvantage.
entries.note: The procedure, and the whole of it is three steps the corpus numbers 4, 5 and 6 -- not a transcription slip: the rendered page prints those numerals, continuing the Rhythm of Play list that precedes it on p. 5. The map records the corpus's numbering and does not renumber. Step 4 is quoted here; steps 5 and 6 are `d20-test-modifiers` and `d20-test-target`, because each states a rule the others do not.

entries.name: What is added to the d20

locator.citation: Playing the Game / D20 Tests / p. 6

crossReferences.cites: See “Proficiency” later in “Playing the Game.”
A class feature, a spell, or another rule might give a bonus or penalty
crossReferences.unmapped: Class features, spells and magic items are outside this slice; each states its own bonus, and the engine takes it as a parameter.

entries.evidence: 5: Add Modifiers. Add these modifiers to the number rolled on the d20: • The Relevant Ability Modifier. “Playing the Game” and “Rules Glossary” explain which ability modifiers to use for various D20 Tests. • Your Proficiency Bonus If Relevant. Each creature has a Proficiency Bonus, a number added when making a D20 Test that uses something, such as a skill, in which the creature has proficiency. See “Proficiency” later in “Playing the Game.” • Circumstantial Bonuses and Penalties. A class feature, a spell, or another rule might give a bonus or penalty to the die roll.
entries.note: Three addends, and the list is closed as printed: the relevant ability modifier, the Proficiency Bonus where it is relevant, and circumstantial bonuses and penalties. The third is the corpus's own open slot -- an engine cannot enumerate it and must accept it from the caller, which is what makes the total honest rather than complete.

entries.name: A D20 Test succeeds when the total equals or exceeds the target number

locator.citation: Playing the Game / D20 Tests / p. 6

crossReferences.cites: (see “Rules Glossary”)
crossReferences.unmapped: The Rules Glossary (pp. 176-191) is outside this map's extent, which is Playing the Game pp. 5-12; trial 8 maps its conditions.

entries.evidence: 6: Compare the Total to a Target Number. If the total of the d20 and its modifiers equals or exceeds the target number, the D20 Test succeeds. Otherwise, it fails. The Game Master determines target numbers and tells players whether their rolls are successful. The target number for an ability check or a saving throw is called a Difficulty Class (DC). The target number for an attack roll is called an Armor Class (AC), which appears on a character sheet or in a stat block (see “Rules Glossary”).
entries.note: Equals or exceeds, so the comparison is >= and a tie succeeds -- the single most consequential arithmetic fact in the slice, and a test must show the boundary. The same sentence names the two target numbers, so this entry defines both terms: a Difficulty Class for a check or a save, an Armor Class for an attack roll. The GM setting target numbers is delegation, recorded in `difficulty-class-set-by-gm`.

entries.name: What an ability check is, and when one is called for

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Ability Checks / p. 6

ambiguity.question: The corpus says an ability check is called for when a creature attempts something 'other than an attack that has a chance of meaningful failure', and when the outcome is 'uncertain and narratively interesting'. Neither 'meaningful failure' nor 'narratively interesting' is measurable, and the same sentence gives the judgement to the GM and the rules jointly. An engine cannot decide that a check is called for; it can only resolve one it is told to make.

entries.evidence: An ability check represents a creature using talent and training to try to overcome a challenge, such as forcing open a stuck door, picking a lock, entertaining a crowd, or deciphering a cipher. The GM and the rules often call for an ability check when a creature attempts something other than an attack that has a chance of meaningful failure. When the outcome is uncertain and narratively interesting, the dice determine the result.
entries.note: The delegation is the rule, not a gap in it: a standard a regulator or a designer wrote deliberately, which trial 1 first recorded. The engine's honest shape is an operation that resolves a check it is given, and no operation that decides one is owed.

entries.name: An ability check is named for the ability modifier it uses

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Ability Checks / Ability Modifier / p. 6

ambiguity.question: Which ability a given check uses is settled by nothing the corpus states: it 'depend[s] on which ability is most relevant', and the Ability Check Examples table gives examples rather than a mapping. For any particular action an engine is asked about, the corpus does not say which of the six applies.

crossReferences.cites: See the Ability Check Examples table

entries.evidence: An ability check is named for the ability modifier it uses: a Strength check, an Intelligence check, and so on. Different ability checks are called for in different situations, depending on which ability is most relevant. See the Ability Check Examples table for examples of each check’s use.
entries.note: The naming is mechanical and the choice is not, and they are one sentence: a Strength check is the check that adds the Strength modifier, whichever action prompted it. A test must show that the engine takes the ability as a parameter and computes the total, and that asking it which ability applies to an action is refused.

entries.name: A relevant proficiency adds the Proficiency Bonus to an ability check

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Ability Checks / Proficiency Bonus / p. 6

ambiguity.question: The bonus applies 'when the GM determines that a skill or tool proficiency is relevant to the check'. Whether a proficiency is relevant to a given check is the GM's, and the corpus states no test for it.

crossReferences.cites: See “Proficiency” later in “Playing the Game”

entries.evidence: Add your Proficiency Bonus to an ability check when the GM determines that a skill or tool proficiency is relevant to the check and you have that proficiency. For example, if a rule refers to a Strength (Acrobatics or Athletics) check, you can add your Proficiency Bonus to the check if you have proficiency in the Acrobatics or Athletics skill. See “Proficiency” later in “Playing the Game” for more information about skill and tool proficiencies.
entries.note: Two conditions, and only one of them is the engine's: the creature has the proficiency, which is a fact it holds, and the GM finds it relevant, which it cannot compute. A test must show the bonus added when both are supplied and withheld when the proficiency is absent.

entries.name: What a saving throw is, and that it is not chosen

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Saving Throws / p. 7

crossReferences.cites: A save’s result is detailed in the effect that caused it
crossReferences.unmapped: The effects that cause saves are spells, monster abilities and hazards, and all but the hazards of p. 12 are outside this slice; each states its own result.

entries.evidence: A saving throw—also called a save—represents an attempt to evade or resist a threat, such as a fiery explosion, a blast of poisonous gas, or a spell trying to invade your mind. You don’t normally choose to make a save; you must make one because your character or a monster (if you’re the GM) is at risk. A save’s result is detailed in the effect that caused it.
entries.note: The defining contrast with an ability check, and the reason both cannot share one shape: a check is attempted and a save is imposed. 'You don't normally choose to make a save' -- an engine is told a save is owed by the effect that caused it, never asked whether to make one.

entries.name: A save may be failed deliberately, without rolling

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Saving Throws / p. 7

entries.evidence: If you don’t want to resist the effect, you can choose to fail the save without rolling.
entries.note: A rule an engine must hold explicitly, because it is the one path through a save that rolls no die: the outcome is a failure the caller elected, not a roll that came out low. A test must show the two are distinguishable in the result.

entries.name: A saving throw is named for the ability modifier it uses

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Saving Throws / Ability Modifier / p. 7

crossReferences.cites: as shown on the Saving Throw Examples table

entries.evidence: Saving throws are named for the ability modifiers they use: a Constitution saving throw, a Wisdom saving throw, and so on. Different saving throws are used to resist different kinds of effects, as shown on the Saving Throw Examples table.
entries.note: The same naming rule as an ability check's, and with a difference that matters: which ability a save uses is settled by the effect that imposes it, not by a judgement of relevance, so this entry is clear where `ability-check-named-for-ability` is ambiguous.

entries.name: A save's DC comes from the effect that caused it, or from the GM

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Saving Throws / Difficulty Class / p. 7

crossReferences.unmapped: Monster abilities (pp. 254-343) and spells are outside this slice; each specifies its own DC.

entries.evidence: The Difficulty Class for a saving throw is determined by the effect that causes it or by the GM. entries.evidence: An attack roll determines whether an attack hits a target. An attack roll hits if the roll equals or exceeds the target’s Armor Class. entries.name: Base AC is 10 plus the Dexterity modifier

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Armor Class / p. 7

crossReferences.unmapped: Armor (Equipment, pp. 83-102), magic items and spells are outside this slice; each states its own modification.

entries.note: The one piece of arithmetic in the slice the corpus states as a formula rather than a table, and it applies to every creature: 10 + Dexterity modifier. A test must show it computed from a score through `ability-modifier-table`, so that the two entries are proved joined.

entries.name: Only one base AC calculation can be in effect

crossReferences.cites: (see “Combat” later in “Playing the Game”)
crossReferences.unmapped: Combat (pp. 13-16) is outside this map's extent and is trial 7's slice, which maps what a Critical Hit does.

entries.evidence: If you roll a 20 on the d20 (called a “natural 20”) for an attack roll, the attack hits regardless of any modifiers or the target’s AC. This is called a Critical Hit (see “Combat” later in “Playing the Game”).
entries.note: An automatic hit that short-circuits `attack-roll-definition` entirely: no total is computed and the AC is not consulted. What a Critical Hit then does is trial 7's; this entry states only that the attack hits and that the hit has that name.

entries.name: A natural 1 on an attack roll misses regardless of modifiers or AC

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Rolling 20 or 1 / p. 7

entries.evidence: If you roll a 1 on the d20 (a “natural 1”) for an attack roll, the attack misses regardless of any modifiers or the target’s AC.
entries.note: The mirror of `natural-20`, and deliberately a separate entry: the corpus states them as two sentences with two outcomes, and one entry holding both would hide that a natural 1 has no named consequence the way a Critical Hit does. Both apply to attack rolls only, which a test must show by leaving a natural 20 on an ability check ordinary.

entries.name: What Advantage and Disadvantage are, and where they come from

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Advantage/Disadvantage / p. 7

crossReferences.cites: You usually acquire Advantage or Disadvantage through the use of special abilities and actions
crossReferences.unmapped: The special abilities are spells, class features and monster abilities, all outside this slice; the actions are on pp. 9-10, inside it, and none of those ten grants Advantage by itself.

entries.evidence: Sometimes a D20 Test is modified by Advantage or Disadvantage. Advantage reflects the positive circumstances surrounding a d20 roll, while Disadvantage reflects negative circumstances. You usually acquire Advantage or Disadvantage through the use of special abilities and actions. The

extraction.renderedReading: The passage ends mid-sentence, at the word 'The'. On the rendered page the sentence continues at the top of the next column -- 'The GM can also decide that circumstances grant Advantage or impose Disadvantage.' -- but that column is printed on p. 8, after the Heroic Inspiration sidebar and the whole of the Proficiency section in the extraction's reading order. The half-sentence is quoted as the extraction gives it.

entries.note: The term trials 7 and 8 both use and neither defines: the combat map's unseen-attacker rules and nine of the fifteen conditions grant or impose one of these, and this is the passage that says what they are. One sentence of this rule is not in this entry, because the extraction puts it two pages of reading order away and 0037 forbids an ellipsis inside a paragraph; it is `advantage-granted-by-gm`, and nothing in the map says the two are one sentence except this note.

entries.name: Advantage or Disadvantage rolls a second d20 and takes the higher or lower

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Roll Two D20s / p. 8

entries.evidence: When a roll has either Advantage or Disadvantage, roll a second d20 when you make the roll. Use the higher of the two rolls if you have Advantage, and use the lower roll if you have Disadvantage. For example, if you have Disadvantage and roll an 18 and a 3, use the 3. If you instead have Advantage and roll those numbers, use the 18.
entries.note: The operation the term names, with the corpus's own worked pair: 18 and 3 gives 3 under Disadvantage and 18 under Advantage. A test must use those numbers, because they are the corpus's demonstration and not the mapper's.

entries.name: Several sources of Advantage, or of Disadvantage, still roll only two d20s

locator.citation: Playing the Game / They Don’t Stack / p. 8

entries.evidence: If multiple situations affect a roll and they all grant Advantage on it, you still roll only two d20s. Similarly, if multiple situations impose Disadvantage on a roll, you roll only two d20s.
entries.note: A counting rule an engine gets wrong by default: sources are collected, and the count of them changes nothing. A test must show three sources of Advantage rolling exactly two dice.

entries.name: Advantage and Disadvantage together cancel, however many of each

locator.citation: Playing the Game / They Don’t Stack / p. 8

entries.evidence: If circumstances cause a roll to have both Advantage and Disadvantage, the roll has neither of them, and you roll one d20. This is true even if multiple circumstances impose Disadvantage and only one grants Advantage or vice versa. In such a situation, you have neither Advantage nor Disadvantage.
entries.note: Cancellation is by presence and never by count -- 'even if multiple circumstances impose Disadvantage and only one grants Advantage'. The corpus states the asymmetric case explicitly because it is the one a reader gets wrong, and a test must use it: three Disadvantages and one Advantage is one d20.

entries.name: A reroll with Advantage or Disadvantage replaces one die, chosen by the roller

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Interactions with Rerolls / p. 8

crossReferences.cites: something in the game lets you reroll or replace the d20
crossReferences.unmapped: The rules that grant a reroll are spells, class features and magic items, outside this slice -- except Heroic Inspiration, which is `heroic-inspiration` on this page and is the example the corpus itself gives.

crossReferences.cites: (see the sidebar below)

entries.evidence: When you have Advantage or Disadvantage and something in the game lets you reroll or replace the d20, you can reroll or replace only one die, not both. You choose which one. For example, if you have Heroic Inspiration (see the sidebar below) and roll a 3 and an 18 on an ability check that has Advantage or Disadvantage, you could expend your Heroic Inspiration to reroll one of those dice, not both of them.
entries.note: Two dice on the table and one may be replaced, by the roller's choice -- so the engine cannot resolve a reroll on its own even when the arithmetic is obvious: which die is a decision it is given. The corpus's worked case is a 3 and an 18 with Heroic Inspiration.

entries.name: Heroic Inspiration is expended to reroll a die, and the new roll stands

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Heroic Inspiration / p. 8

entries.evidence: Sometimes the GM or a rule gives you Heroic Inspiration. If you have Heroic Inspiration, you can expend it to reroll any die immediately after rolling it, and you must use the new roll.
entries.note: 'Any die', not any d20: the only reroll in the slice that reaches a damage die or a hit die as well. And the new roll stands -- an engine may not keep the better of the two, which is the mistake a test must catch.

entries.name: Never more than one Heroic Inspiration, and a duplicate may be given away

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Heroic Inspiration / p. 8

entries.evidence: Only One at a Time. You can never have more than one instance of Heroic Inspiration. If something gives you Heroic Inspiration and you already have it, you can give it to a player character in your group who lacks it.
entries.note: A capacity of one, and a transfer rule that fires on the overflow: the second instance is not discarded, it may be handed to a player character in the group who has none. A test must show the count never exceeding one and the overflow being offered rather than lost. The corpus prints the rule under a run-in heading, bold at the head of its own paragraph, and the extraction gives no line of its own for it -- so the heading path cannot name it and the citation stops at the section above. #435.

entries.name: The GM awards Heroic Inspiration, and other rules may grant it

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Heroic Inspiration / p. 8

crossReferences.cites: Other rules might allow your character to gain Heroic Inspiration
crossReferences.unmapped: The rule the corpus names is the Human species trait (Character Origins, p. 83 onward), outside this slice.

entries.evidence: Gaining Heroic Inspiration. Your GM can give you Heroic Inspiration for a variety of reasons. Typically, GMs award it when you do something particularly heroic, in character, or entertaining. It’s a reward for making the game more fun for everyone playing. Other rules might allow your character to gain Heroic Inspiration independent of the GM’s decision. For example, Human characters start each day with Heroic Inspiration.
entries.note: An assertion and not an ambiguity, which is the distinction trial 1 drew: 'particularly heroic, in character, or entertaining' is not a standard the engine must resolve and fails to -- it is the GM's judgement arriving as a parameter, and the engine's whole duty is to demand it, record who gave it, and never infer it. The second half is the half an engine can act on alone: other rules grant Heroic Inspiration without the GM, and the corpus names Human characters starting each day with it, outside this slice. The corpus prints the rule under a run-in heading, bold at the head of its own paragraph, and the extraction gives no line of its own for it -- so the heading path cannot name it and the citation stops at the section above. #435.

entries.name: Every creature has a Proficiency Bonus, and where it comes from

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Proficiency / p. 8

crossReferences.cites: (described in “Character Creation”)
crossReferences.unmapped: Character Creation (pp. 19-23) is outside this map's extent, which ends at p. 12; a character's level is settled there.

crossReferences.cites: (see “Rules Glossary”)
crossReferences.unmapped: The Rules Glossary (pp. 176-191) is outside this map's extent; trial 8 maps its conditions, and Challenge Rating is not among them.

crossReferences.cites: The Proficiency Bonus table shows how the bonus is determined

entries.evidence: All creatures have a Proficiency Bonus, which reflects the impact that training has on the creature’s capabilities. A character’s Proficiency Bonus increases as the character gains levels (described in “Character Creation”). A monster’s Proficiency Bonus is based on its Challenge Rating (see “Rules Glossary”). The Proficiency Bonus table shows how the bonus is determined.
entries.note: The term four entries in this slice already add -- on a check, a save, an attack and a spell save DC -- and this is where the corpus says what it is. One number per creature, from level for a character and from Challenge Rating for a monster, and both sources are outside the slice: the engine takes the level or the CR and reads the table.

entries.name: The Proficiency Bonus for each level or Challenge Rating

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Proficiency Bonus / p. 8

extraction.renderedReading: p. 8 prints the table as two side-by-side 'Level or CR'/Bonus column pairs: Up to 4/+2, 5–8/+3, 9–12/+4, 13–16/+5 in the left pair and 17–20/+6, 21–24/+7, 25–28/+8, 29–30/+9 in the right. The extraction reads each printed line across both pairs, so its order is Up to 4 +2 17–20 +6, then 5–8 +3 21–24 +7.

entries.note: A finite table, so the whole of it is quoted and never a sample: eight bands from 'Up to 4' through 29–30, and a test must assert the whole mapping. 'Up to 4' is open at the bottom and the corpus gives no floor, so a Challenge Rating of 0 takes +2 by the band's own words and not by an inference the map supplies.

entries.name: When the Proficiency Bonus is applied

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Proficiency / p. 8

entries.evidence: This bonus is applied to a D20 Test when the creature has proficiency in a skill, in a saving throw, or with an item that the creature uses to make the D20 Test. The bonus is also used for spell attacks and for calculating the DC of saving throws for spells.
entries.note: The general statement the three per-test rules on pp. 6-7 instantiate -- a skill, a save, or an item used to make the test -- plus two applications that are not D20 Tests at all: spell attacks, and the DC of a saving throw a spell imposes. The second is the only place in the slice where the bonus is added to something other than a roll.

entries.name: The Proficiency Bonus is never added twice to one number

locator.citation: Playing the Game / The Bonus Doesn’t Stack / p. 8

entries.evidence: Your Proficiency Bonus can’t be added to a die roll or another number more than once.
entries.note: The counterpart of `advantage-does-not-stack` for the other thing an engine would naturally accumulate. A test must show two relevant proficiencies on one check adding the bonus once.

entries.name: The GM may grant Advantage or impose Disadvantage

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Advantage/Disadvantage / p. 8

entries.evidence: GM can also decide that circumstances grant Advantage or impose Disadvantage.
entries.note: The second half of `advantage-disadvantage`'s last sentence, and a separate entry only because the extraction separates them: the quote begins mid-sentence, at 'GM', because the article that governs it is printed on p. 7. An assertion -- the GM's decision reaches the engine as a parameter, and the engine records who granted it.
